prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

A man in a high-rise apartment confronts vertigo and urban alienation by mentally cataloging the building’s security, amenities, lease terms, and physical sensations to reassure himself that reality remains normal and measurable. Yet the imagined swamp rising inch by inch beneath him exposes the fragility of that ordered, commodified world and suggests an uncontrollable reality steadily encroaching upon it.

outputs.L1: He walked to the window and stared down twenty stories toward the street, gaseous and dizzy as a swamp—not visible from this height, though there had been a street down there, and he knew it. It came with the apartment: the guarded foyers and halls; the doorman, holstered beneath the uniform; the television split-screening the front and rear entrances. He knew it was all there, and he was here, twenty stories above the unsettled swamp-mist. He knew the trucks bound for the bridge were still passing nearby; he could feel them rumbling through the soles of his feet. So he knew the floor he walked on was someone’s ceiling, and it was all normal tonight and countable: a two-year lease, because a desirable apartment with a full view of the river—a five-by-three balcony through the door—is a $200 deposit, fully carpeted, with a self-defrosting refrigerator. The balcony door is stuck, but he can stare twenty stories down from the windowsill, watching the swamp-smoke curl and thin, the swamp lapping at the base, and the unpaid-for miracle rising one inch at a time.
outputs.L2:
He crossed to the window and looked toward the ground, twenty floors below. The street could not be seen from this height; it seemed to dissolve into a sickening, vaporous marsh. Still, he knew a street existed down there. It belonged to the apartment’s arrangement as surely as the secured lobby and corridors, the doorman carrying a gun beneath his uniform, and the television monitor displaying both entrances at once. All of it remained below, while he stood twenty stories above the restless fog of the swamp.

Nearby, trucks headed for the bridge continued to pass. Their vibration traveled up through his feet, reminding him that the floor beneath him served as another person’s ceiling. Everything tonight was ordinary, measurable, and itemized: a two-year lease; a desirable apartment with an unobstructed river view; a five-by-three-foot balcony beyond the door; a $200 deposit; wall-to-wall carpeting; a refrigerator that defrosted itself—

The balcony door would not open. Even so, he could lean at the window and gaze down twenty stories, watching the marsh vapor coil and fade, the swamp wash against the building’s foundation, and the miracle he had not yet paid for advance inch by inch.
outputs.L3:
He stands at the window of his twentieth-story apartment, staring down at the place where the street should be. Instead, a dizzying, swamp-like mist churns below, swallowing the pavement and blurring the city into something strange and unrecognizable.

Inside the building, everything still suggests security and routine. The entrances are guarded, an armed doorman watches the lobby, and surveillance cameras monitor the halls. These familiar protections preserve an appearance of normalcy, even as the world outside seems to be disappearing. Beneath his feet, the rumble of traffic crossing the bridge offers further reassurance. Its steady vibration tells him that the street remains somewhere below and that the lower floors are still standing and occupied.

To calm himself, he mentally catalogs the apartment’s practical details: the terms of the lease, the river view, the balcony, the carpeting, and the appliances. Each feature is concrete and measurable, evidence of an ordinary life governed by contracts, amenities, and familiar possessions. Yet these details cannot hold back what is happening. The mist—or perhaps a rising swamp—continues to climb around the building. When he tries the balcony door, he finds it stuck, sealing him inside. Beyond the glass, the encroaching water rises steadily, making it impossible to deny that a disaster is unfolding.
outputs.L4:
At the window, Daniel kept one hand pressed against the glass and named the things that could not possibly fail.

The pane was laminated, double-glazed, rated to withstand winds far stronger than anything forecast that evening. The balcony door was locked at three points. The building had two emergency stairwells, six elevators, sprinklers in every room, smoke detectors linked directly to the concierge desk, and cameras covering the lobby, garage, loading bay, mailroom, and all residential corridors. His lease specified twenty-four-hour security. It also included access to the gym, the rooftop garden, the heated pool, and a private storage cage on Level B3.

He repeated these facts while looking down.

Thirty-two floors below, traffic moved between the towers in bright, orderly threads. From this height, buses seemed to glide rather than shudder, and pedestrians became dark marks crossing illuminated grids. The city had been measured, zoned, paved, priced, and insured. Every square foot belonged to someone. Every window corresponded to a unit number, every unit number to a contract, every contract to a payment schedule.

Daniel reminded himself that he occupied Apartment 3208 until the final day of September, with the option to renew at the prevailing market rate.

His breathing slowed.

The sensation in his legs was only vertigo: a disagreement between the eyes and the inner ear. The pressure in his chest was muscular. The dampness on his palms came from an ordinary stress response. All of it could be named. Anything that could be named could be located within a system, and anything within a system could be managed.

He stepped back from the glass.

The apartment was exactly as advertised: engineered oak flooring, stone counters, recessed lighting, integrated appliances, climate control divided into three zones. Even the silence was part of the rent. The windows excluded sirens, engines, arguments, and rain, leaving only a faint mechanical hum from the ventilation system.

Then he smelled mud.

It was not the sourness of a blocked drain or the mineral odor of wet concrete. It was darker and richer: stagnant water, crushed reeds, decaying leaves. The smell seemed to rise through the floorboards.

Daniel checked the kitchen sink. Dry. He opened the cabinet beneath it and touched the pipes. No leak. He inspected the dishwasher seal, the washing machine hose, the shower drain, and the narrow space behind the toilet. Everything was clean.

In the hallway, he pressed the elevator button and watched the numbers descend.

31.  
30.  
29.

For a moment he imagined the shaft not as a column of steel and concrete but as a hollow reed sunk deep into black water.

The doors opened. No one was inside.

Daniel did not enter.

He returned to the apartment and locked the door, though it had already been locked. On the building’s resident portal he opened the maintenance page. There were categories for plumbing, electrical faults, heating, ventilation, appliance repair, pests, access cards, noise complaints, and miscellaneous concerns. He selected plumbing, then reconsidered. The smell did not belong to plumbing. It belonged to somewhere without pipes.

He closed the page.

Outside, evening gathered between the towers. The roads below had begun to shine, although no rain had fallen. Daniel leaned toward the window, careful not to touch it this time.

The streets were gone.

In their place lay a flat expanse of dark water, broken by clumps of grass and the pale trunks of drowned trees. Traffic lights stood above the surface like colored lanterns. The roofs of cars formed small islands. Something broad and slow moved where the intersection had been, bending the reeds without revealing itself.

Daniel shut his eyes.

The city map remained in his mind: four blocks to the metro, two to the supermarket, one to the pharmacy. Elevation above sea level: forty-six meters. Building height: one hundred and twenty-eight meters. Apartment area: eighty-one square meters, excluding balcony.

He opened his eyes.

The roads had returned. Taxis turned at the intersection. A cyclist waited beside a delivery van. The world was dry, hard-edged, and available for purchase.

Still, the smell persisted.

That night he lay awake cataloging physical sensations. Cool air against his face. Cotton sheet over his legs. Mattress supporting shoulders, spine, hips, heels. Pulse regular. Tongue dry. No fever. No tremor.

Beneath these facts, he heard frogs.

Their calls rose through the building in irregular waves. He pictured water entering the underground garage, covering the painted arrows and reserved bays, lifting loose receipts from the concrete. It would climb past B3, where his storage cage held two suitcases and a box of tax documents. It would reach B2, then B1, swallowing electrical conduits and charging stations. The pumps would activate. Alarms would sound. Engineers would arrive with equipment and forms.

But in his imagination no alarms sounded. The water rose silently, one inch at a time.

By dawn it had reached the lobby. It slid over marble tiles, softened the legs of designer chairs, and carried leaves against the concierge desk. The security monitors continued to display their empty corridors. The turnstiles blinked green beneath the surface.

Daniel stood at the window again.

The city looked normal. That was almost worse. The towers shone with morning light, sealed and immaculate, while below them the swamp waited—not as a disaster, but as a correction. It had no lease, no access code, no assessed value. It recognized neither property lines nor evacuation plans. It did not hurry. It did not need to.

He placed his palm against the glass and felt the faint vibration of the building.

For a few seconds he could not tell whether the tower was swaying in the wind or settling into mud.

Then the elevator chimed in the corridor, the ventilation system sighed, and somewhere far beneath him, steady and patient, water rose another inch.
outputs.L5: He walked to the edge of the quiet lake, where the morning mist drifted above the water. In his hand, he carried a letter he had read a hundred times. The path behind him led back to everything familiar, while the distant hills promised uncertainty and change. He paused, listened to the wind moving through the trees, and finally understood that some journeys begin with a single brave decision. Folding the letter carefully, he placed it in his pocket and continued forward.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal stream-of-consciousness paragraph about a man looking down from a twentieth-floor apartment as the city below seems to dissolve into a swamp. Use minimal punctuation and blur together real-estate language, security details, and hallucination.
counterfactuals.output: He stands behind the floor to ceiling glass of the twentieth floor premium corner unit with keycard access and twenty four hour surveillance watching the avenues soften into black water while traffic lights blink like feverish frogs and the concierge whispers through the intercom that all exits are secure all deposits nonrefundable as cypress knees push through the parking garage and the lobby fills with warm green mist where marble was recently renovated where the doorman sinks smiling beneath the lilies and somewhere below a siren becomes a heron becomes a sales agent promising unobstructed views even as the skyline folds into reeds and the elevator dings behind him though no one has clearance though something wet is breathing in the hall and the listing said move in ready the listing said flood zone unknown the listing said this height would keep him safe

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental literary passage in the style of fragmented postmodern fiction. Include a high-rise window, a guarded foyer, bridge traffic rumbling underfoot, a stuck balcony door, and swamp mist consuming the street.
counterfactuals.output:
The high-rise window kept revising the city.

First: towers, sodium lamps, a river stitched shut with reflections.

Then: nothing but swamp mist consuming the street—traffic lights fading greenly inside it, cars becoming rumors, pedestrians erased from the knees upward.

*

In the guarded foyer, the night clerk sat behind glass, reading yesterday’s newspaper backward.

“No visitors,” he said.

“I live here.”

“That’s what they all say.”

His uniform had no insignia, only a small damp patch spreading over the heart.

*

On the nineteenth floor, the balcony door was stuck.

She pulled. I pushed. Or I pulled and she had already left; chronology is another door swollen in its frame.

Beyond the glass, a plastic chair trembled in the wind.

OPEN, said the handle.

NO, said the building.

*

Bridge traffic rumbling underfoot, although the bridge was three blocks east and forty meters below. The floor carried every truck through the apartment: cups ticking in cupboards, teeth meeting teeth, a vase inching toward the ledge.

We lay down to listen.

Inside the concrete, thousands of engines passed without arriving.

*

By midnight the mist reached the foyer.

The guard unlocked nothing.

The elevator descended with its doors open, full of reeds.

On the nineteenth floor, the high-rise window displayed a white, depthless field. The stuck balcony door gave one soft knock from the other side.

Then another.

As if the outside wanted in.

As if it had always lived here.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe a tenant experiencing vertigo and alienation in an expensive city apartment, using a single breathless paragraph with run-on sentences, abrupt capitalization, and snippets from a rental advertisement.
counterfactuals.output: The floor tilts whenever the upstairs neighbor drags a chair across the ceiling, or maybe it is the whole city tipping toward the river, and I grip the quartz countertop—LUXURY FINISHES, SUN-DRENCHED OPEN CONCEPT—while sirens comb the avenue thirty floors below and the windows refuse to open more than four inches, for safety, they said, as if safety were laminated glass and a doorman who never remembers my name, and every room appears wider in the listing, BRIGHT AND AIRY, PERFECT FOR ENTERTAINING, though nobody visits because the elevator makes them nauseous and I have begun to forget which reflections are mine, the mirrored closet doubling the bed, the bed doubling the rent, the rent doubling the pulse behind my eyes, NO FEE, they promised, then came the amenity fee, the move-in fee, the key fee, the fee for breathing climate-controlled air in a building where I know no one, ABSOLUTELY NO PETS, and at night the skyline spins like a chandelier coming loose, all those expensive windows lit with other solitary people staring outward, inward, nowhere, and I whisper STUNNING VIEWS, STUNNING VIEWS, STUNNING VIEWS until the walls lean close enough to hear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dystopian prose-poem where a man reassures himself that his apartment building and the street below are normal and measurable, even as a primordial swamp rises around them inch by inch.
counterfactuals.output:
The building has twelve floors. He counts them every morning from the pavement upward, though the pavement is no longer visible. Twelve floors, eight windows each, four windows lit before dawn. These are facts. Facts have edges. Facts do not hatch.

The street below is thirty feet wide from curb to curb. He remembers the yellow line precisely, remembers parking meters, hydrants, the bus stop where a woman once dropped a paper bag of oranges. Nothing has changed, he tells himself, except the water. An inch at midnight. Another by breakfast. Water is measurable.

At first it gathered in the gutters, black and glossy as spilled film. Then reeds appeared through the storm drains. Horsetails. Ferns with fists that opened overnight. The city sent notices advising residents to remain calm and avoid contact with unauthorized vegetation. He taped the notices to his refrigerator in chronological order.

The elevator still descends, although its doors now open on a warm green darkness. Somewhere beneath the lobby, something enormous exhales. Bubbles rise through the mailboxes.

He stands at his window with a ruler.

The swamp has reached the second-floor fire escape. It bears the moon in pieces. Pale insects skate across its surface, each one too large to name politely. Vines soften the traffic lights. A heron, taller than a lamppost, waits where the pharmacy stood, its eye fixed on an age before walls.

The building is plumb, he says.

The street is straight.

North is north.

He writes the measurements in a ledger: waterline, 14 feet 3 inches; humidity, 96 percent; distance from glass to nearest blossom, 7 inches. The blossom turns toward him as he writes. Its petals are the color of old teeth.

From the apartments above come the ordinary sounds of life: a chair dragged across a ceiling, a baby crying, someone practicing scales on a piano gone slowly out of tune. From below come other sounds, also ordinary, if repeated often enough: the slap of tails, the click of mandibles, the low communal croaking that occasionally shapes itself into his name.

He locks the window.

He checks the lock.

A lock is a mechanism with two positions.

By evening, roots have entered the stairwell. By morning, they have learned the handrails. Moss covers the emergency exit map but leaves visible the red words YOU ARE HERE.

He finds this reassuring.

Here is a place.

Here can be measured.

Outside, the primordial water rises another inch, lifting taxis, benches, bones. The towers across the avenue stand reflected in it, trembling, as if remembering they were trees.

He draws a careful line on the wall.

Just above it, he writes: NORMAL.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an unpunctuated, hallucinatory urban scene that contrasts the countable comforts of a two-year lease—doorman, cameras, carpeting, refrigerator, river view—with an unpaid-for natural miracle overtaking the building.
counterfactuals.output:
two years promised in the paper dream

one doorman beneath the brass moon  
six cameras blinking their red seeds  
twelve floors of obedient carpeting  
one refrigerator humming winter into milk  
one river view framed and numbered

then the miracle arrived without invoice

moss lifted the lobby tiles  
ferns unrolled from every keyhole  
silver fish swam through the elevators  
and roots entered the walls like green lightning

the doorman became a tree full of sparrows  
the cameras opened into black flowers  
the carpeting rippled with meadow wind  
the refrigerator hatched blue moths  
the river climbed out of its view

by morning the whole building was breathing leaves  
and no one could count what they owed
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
